comment.value:
This paper presents BIPNN (Binary Integer Programming Neural Network), an unsupervised learning framework to solve nonlinear BIP problems via hypergraph neural networks. This work converts constrained BIP problems with nonlinear ($\sin$, $\log$, $\exp$) terms into a polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) formalism, and then uses a continuous-annealing-enhanced unsupervised training pipeline leveraging hypergraph neural networks to minimize the PUBO objective. It further proposes a GPU-acceleration algorithm to improve computational efficiency. An empirical study of the performance of BIPNN is provided on synthetic hypergraphs (up to thousands of variables) and real-world graph/hypergraph max-cut benchmarks.


Strengths:
* The paper combines polynomial reformulation, hypergraph modeling, and unsupervised learning into a novel, end-to-end framework for the challenging class of nonlinear BIP problems.
* The GPU-accelerated PUBO loss formulation addresses an important computational bottleneck.
* The algorithm is evaluated extensively.  BIPNN matches or outperforms other approaches (SCIP and Tabu) in solution quality, while scaling reasonably in terms of solution time under fixed GPU resources. During the rebuttal period, the authors additionally compared against Gurobi, showing comparable quality of results on small-/medium-scale problems, and ability to find solutions under a reasonable time budget in large-scale scenarios where Gurobi could not.


Weaknesses:
* The method is limited to simple nonlinear terms such as $\sin$ and $\log$. The general transformation for multivariate nonlinearities can incur exponential preprocessing in the number of variables per term; the paper does not address this more general setting.


Other major points of discussion:
* Reviewer FymU pointed out that the HyperGNN architectural choices were not well justified. The authors provided a comparison of different HyperGNN models in their response, and indicated they would include this in the appendix.
* Reviewer d2xH raised questions about the impact of prediction errors. The authors clarified that they include a (small) safety margin on constraints.
* Several reviewers indicated that the paper does not adequately differentiate itself from recent and similar work using hypergraphs for optimization. The authors provided a comparative table of methods and indicated why the prior literature is developed for different or more specialized settings.
* There was significant back-and-forth about initial lack of comparison to Gurobi, which the authors initially claimed was not applicable to BIPs, but later realized was. Upon this, the authors followed up with additional comparisons to Gurobi. Some reviewers felt this sufficiently improved the quality of experiments; other reviewers felt the comparisons were still insufficient, and more generally that the authors' lack of knowledge about Gurobi handling this problem setting had affected their confidence in the authors' knowledge of this area and therefore the paper's technical claims.


Overall, considering both the initial submission and rebuttal, the paper provides an interesting and convincing algorithm to an important class of problems, differentiates itself from prior literature, and provides informative experimental comparisons against strong baselines. I therefore recommend acceptance.

**We thank all reviewers and ACs for their time and efforts.**

> Novelty

BIPNN's novelty was noted by the reviewers. Designing unsupervised neural solvers for general nonlinear BIPs faces challenges. In this paper, we clarify these challenges. We believe that some ideas in BIPNN—such as polynomial reformulation, unconstrained reformulation, and GPU-accelerated PUBO solvers—are helpful for the community of neural CO to better understand binary programming problems.

> Experiments

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback.

> Question 1: Gurobi can solver nonlinear BIP problems, including polynomial and non-polynomial (e.g., log, sin). I suggest authors to try it again.

Recent Gurobi 12.0 has begun supporting nonlinear BIPs.

We consulted the Gurobi Optimizer Reference Manual (https://docs.gurobi.com/_/downloads/optimizer/en/12.0/pdf/). As it described in Para. 7, Sec. 1.3, "The available objective types are linear, piecewise-linear, quadratic (both convex and non-convex), and multi-objective." This description misled us.

For the hypergraph max-cut problem, we solved it by introducing auxiliary variables and constraints.​​ We have already presented comparative experimental results in our previous response.
|Method|BAT|EAT|UAT|DBLP|	CiteSeer|Primary|High|Cora|
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
|GUROBI|**655**	|**3997**	|8431	|**2869**	|**3960**	|8448	|5195	|**1400**|
|SCIP	|**655**	|3849	|7899	|**2869**	|**3960**	|7603	|4599	|1215|
|Tabu	|652	|3970	|8402	|2710	|3717	|8500	|5160	|1360|
|BIPNN	|653	|**3997**	|**8463**	|2847	|3944	|**8516**	|**5252**	|1397|

Moreover, we find that for general nonlinear BIPs, the PUBO (Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization) objective function can be ​​manually reformulated using auxiliary variables and linear constraints​​. Thus, we refine our prior conclusion regarding Gurobi’s capability to solve nonlinear BIP problems and supplement it with the following experimental results.
| Number of Variables | SCIP | Gurobi| BIPNN |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| 3000 | -700 | **-810** |   -771  |
| 4000 | -876 | -1003  | **-1064**   |
| 5000 |  -1034  | -1289  | **-1342**  |

The table shows optimization results of different methods on the objective function, with computation time constrained to half an hour. The number of variables ranges between 3,000–5,000 and the number of monomials is twice the variable count. The degree of each monomial is 6.

> Question 2: The papers I suggested such as MCPG can solver general nonlinear BIPs. MCPG provides the methods for these kind of problems, such as max-cut, including the filters.

Through a careful examination of the paper, we think that MCPG could potentially be extended to general nonlinear BIPs. However, the authors currently only provide implementations for QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization) problems (https://github.com/optsuite/MCPG/blob/9255b46f3fc0aa9e6f0097e82fa684538695c178/src/cpp/README.md).

1. We consider that solving PUBO (Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization) with this approach would require additional design and implementation efforts (e.g., the parameter selection for λ in Eq. 6, inequality constraints Eq. 2). BIPNN has completed partial work including the polynomial and unconstrained reformulation methods, which have potential to be combined with more efficient PUBO solvers (e.g., MCPG). Further investigation will be conducted in our future work.

2. It should be emphasized that we tested the max-cut problem using the implementation provided by the authors of MCPG, and the results were indeed very good. Thus, the prospect is promising.

We are happy to provide additional clarifications and engage further in the discussions.

Many thanks, The Authors.

Thank you to the authors for their exceptionally detailed rebuttal and for the considerable effort invested in addressing my concerns. I especially appreciate the follow-up comment correcting the information about Gurobi's capabilities, which demonstrates diligence and a commitment to accuracy.

The rebuttal has successfully resolved the major questions I had about the paper:

1. On Novelty and Positioning (Q3): The detailed comparison table and the point-by-point discussion have effectively clarified the novelty of BIPNN and its positioning relative to prior works like NeuralQP and HypOp. This has resolved my concerns about the paper's originality.

2. On the Unsupervised Approach (Q4): The data-backed justification for choosing an unsupervised method, highlighting the prohibitive computational cost of generating labels for general nonlinear BIPs, is compelling and well-argued.

3. On Empirical Evaluation (Q5): This was my primary concern, and the authors' response here was outstanding. The new experiments are a significant addition and were crucial to my reassessment. The results comparing BIPNN against both SCIP and Gurobi on the reformulated hypergraph max-cut problem and, more importantly, on new general nonlinear BIP instances, have successfully demonstrated the method's practical effectiveness. This is precisely the kind of empirical validation I was hoping to see.

Given that the authors' comprehensive responses and, critically, the new empirical evidence have fully resolved my initial reservations, I have raised my score to positive. The paper is now in a much stronger position, and I believe it makes a valuable contribution to the field.

We thank the reviewer for their careful reading and comments. We address the weaknesses they mentioned below.
> Weakness 1: The precise "one-to-one" mapping between polynomial BIP objectives and hypergraph structures is mentioned multiple times throughout the text and in the abstract and while this mapping is somewhat intuitive from figure 1 it is not described precisely in the text. When the authors mention this in the abstract it gives the impression that there will be some mathematical results/ that shows the existence of this mapping. More details about this would be beneficial.

We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback. Indeed the observation of mapping correspondence between polynomials and hypergraphs structures is crucial for understanding BIPNN. We will augment the caption of Fig. 1 with the following description:

As shown in c and d, BIPNN's hypergraph modeling (Sec. 3.1) stems from the key observation that when variables are treated as nodes, any monomial with coefficient $1$ can be represented as a hyperedge, while polynomials can be expressed through hypergraphs – and vice versa.

> Weakness 2: A brief description of the inner workings of HyperGNNs would be useful to clarify these models for less familiar readers.

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback. The following descriptions will be incorporated into Sec. 3.2:

HyperGNNs​ are graph-based deep learning architectures that generalize GNNs to operate on hypergraphs. These HyperGNN models includes HGNN, HGNN+, HyperGCN, UniGCN (or UniGAT, UniSAGE, UniGIN). We have tested these models and observed that HGNN+ always outperformed other methods. Thus in this work we use HGNN+ to build BIPNN. The $l$-th convolutional layer of HGNN is built as below:

$X^{(l)}={\rm ReLU}{(D_v^{-\frac{1}{2}}HWD_e^{-1}H^TD_v^{-\frac{1}{2}}X^{(l-1)}\Theta ^{(l)})}$

where $X^{(l)}$ is the embedding matrix generated by the $l$-th convolutional layer.
For a vertex $v_i$ in the hypergraph, the degree is defined as $\mathrm{deg}(v_i)=\sum_{e_j\in E}{H_{ij}}$.
Similarly, the degree of an edge $e_j\in E$ is defined as $\mathrm{deg}(e_j)=\sum_{v_i\in V}{H_{ij}}$.
$D_v$ and $D_e$ are used to denote the diagonal matrices of the vertex degrees and edge degrees, respectively.
$W=\mathrm{diag}(|e_1|,...,|e_{|E|}|)$ can be regrarded as the weight of hyperedges.
The parameter $\Theta^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d^{(l-1)}\times d^{(l)}}$ is learned during training.

> Weakness 3: While the training workflow is clear from the text and highly useful Fig 1, I feel like the paper would benefit from a brief intuitive explanation of how Eq. 4 works with the training.

We will provide the following explanation for Eq. 4:

Eq. 4 transforms the computation of large-scale polynomials into efficient matrix operations. It leverages PyTorch-supported broadcasting mechanisms to distribute the vector of decision variables across each monomial (hyperedge), enabling parallel computation.

> Question 1: The authors use the term "matrix" to refer to the PUBO matrix Q but this seems to be simply the vector of coefficients, naming it "matrix" introduces a bit of confusion so maybe "vector" would be a better term for clarity.

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback. We will fix this problem.

> Question 2: How exactly does BIPNN generate a new hypergraph structure as opposed to the original hypergraph (Fig 3 & Sections 5 & 6)? This seems to be a central point in the experiments section but the phenomenon isn't clearly described. A brief discussion of how the generated hypergraph differs from the original one (perhaps with an example) would be beneficial.

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback. The following descriptions will be incorporated into Sec. 6.3:

Unlike conventional machine learning tasks (e.g., node classification), we hypothesize that the hypergraph structure for BIPNN should be related to the loss function. Thus HGNN's energy flow directs each polynomial term along proper gradient paths.



> Question 3: What exactly is the ratio of solutions? (Fig 4 & Section 6) Are the solutions here on the max-cut problem therefore the "solution" is the number of cuts and higher is better or is it the cost-function of the PUBO problem? This is unclear from the text.

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback. The following modification will be applied to line 251: $O_{\rm BIPNN}^{s}$ and $O_{\rm SCIP}^{s}$ are solutions (the number of cuts) obtained by BIPNN and SCIP.

We thank the reviewers for their feedback. We believe we have addressed the reviewer’s main concerns of this paper. We are happy to provide additional clarifications and engage further in the discussions if we have misunderstood any crucial points.

Many thanks, The Authors.

> Limitation 1: In abstract, authors said “Yet, they lack scalability for tackling nonlinear challenges”, however, I did not see the contribution on scalability.

The scalability of BIPNN lies in two aspects:
1. It is computationally efficient. In Fig. 6, we demonstrate that without using BIPNN's fast algorithm   (Fig. 1 at the bottom), the computation time for the polynomial objective function during forward propagation grows rapidly as the problem size increases.
2. Polynomial reformulation of various nonlinear terms. It employs polynomial reformulation to transform simple nonlinear terms (e.g., $\rm{sin}$, $\rm{log}$) into polynomials (Sec. 4). This is crucial because BIPNN provides a fast computational framework for polynomial objective functions.

> Limitation 2: what’s PUBO?

PUBO is Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization, we clarified it in ​​Footnote 1 on Page 2​​.

> Limitation 3: in abstract, “reformulates BIPs-constrained, discrete, and nonlinear (sin, log, exp) optimization problems-into unconstrained, differentiable, and polynomial loss functions”, the eqn 7 may be not differentiable.

On line 172, we explicitly state the non-differentiability of Eq. 7. This is why we use ReLU-based penalty method (line 174).
However, if polynomial reformulation is adopted (see Appendix B), the polynomial penalty terms (line 176) will be differentiable.

To ensure the accuracy of the description, we will revise it as "​​differentiable (almost everywhere)".

> Limitation 4: the performance evaluation, plz compare the SOTA solver such as GUROBI, and several RL methods such as [1] .

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback. **Gurobi does not support solving general nonlinear BIP problems. Gurobi is designed to solve linear programming (LP) and quadratic programming (QP)**. It cannot handle cubic or higher-degree polynomials (e.g., $x₁x₂x₃$), and non-convex QP problems. While SCIP is outperformed by Gurobi in solving LP and QP problems, SCIP provides capabilities for handling general non-linear BIP problems. We tested Gurobi's performance on QPLIB and found that Gurobi solves QP problems with extremely high efficiency.

The reviewer ​​observes​​ that penalty methods have been previously applied [1], [2]. Penalty methods are well-known techniques in CO. BIPNN's core innovation is that it introduces a method to map constraints (e.g., $x₁+3x₂-2<0$) to continuously differentiable polynomial penalties (QUBO or PUBO formalism), such as $x₂+x₁x₂$ or more simplified form $x₂$. The advantages lie in two aspects:
1. Quantum annealers (e.g., D-Wave systems) can efficiently solve QUBO and PUBO problems. Our method thus extends quantum computing's applicability.

[1] Differentiable Integer Linear Programming\
[2] HypOp: Distributed constrained combinatorial optimization leveraging hypergraph neural networks\
[3] NeuralQP: A general hypergraph-based optimization framework for large-scale qcqps\
[4] A Monte Carlo Policy Gradient Method with Local Search for Binary Optimization\
[5] Supplementing recurrent neural networks with annealing to solve combinatorial optimization problems

1. DiffILO [1]. DiffILO is an unsupervised method with performance that can exceed Gurobi. Its methodology is the most similar to that of BIPNN. However, DiffILO employs bipartite graphs and GNNs to model constraints, whereas BIPNN utilizes HyperGNN to represent nonlinear BIPs. DiffILO is designed for linear BIPs, while BIPNN primarily addresses general nonlinear BIPs. Thus, our comparative analysis focuses on SCIP.

2. HypOp [2]. HypOp is an unsupervised methods. Compared with HypOp, ​​BIPNN first discovers the mapping correspondence between polynomials and hypergraphs structures​​. Compared to linear and quadratic problems, ​​the core challenge in solving nonlinear BIPs lies in exploiting GPU acceleration during training​​. BIPNN proposes a computational framework specifically for this purpose. ​​In contrast, HypOp utilizes distributed HyperGNN training​​, yet its hypergraph modeling solely targets constraints rather than objective functions, thus rendering HypOp ​​inapplicable to general BIP problems.

3. NeuralQP [3]. It is supervised and designed for QP problems. Supervised learning methods​​ require precomputing vast amounts of labels[1]. Obtaining labels for nonlinear BIPs is challenging, since ​​SCIP has higher computational overhead when solving nonlinear BIPs. Although NeuralQP demonstrates strong performance, it is specifically designed for QP problems. In contrast, BIPNN is designed for solving more complex nonlinear BIP problems, making it inherently difficult to match the performance of specialized QP solvers​​ such as NeuralQP.

4. MCPG [4] and VCA [5]. Reinforcement learning methods typically exhibit slow training convergence. MCPG [4] improves reinforcement learning algorithms and achieves strong performance on three problems: graph max-cut, MIMO, and MaxSAT. VCA also demonstrates its performance on TSP and graph max-cut problems. However, we observe that these studies exclusively evaluate on specific CO problems, making it difficult to assess whether their methods generalize to general BIPs.

For example, it seems that MCPG requires designing customized filters for specific problems, and we don't understand how to create filters for hypergraph max-cut or general BIP problems. BIPNN's novel GPU acceleration techniques; polynomial reformulation; and unconstrained optimization mechanisms may potentially enhance other methods. 

In summary, BIPNN is proposed for general nonlinear BIPs, and it is fast. We believe ​​BIPNN and DiffILO collectively address numerous limitations inherent in penalty-based deep learning methods​​ for solving nonlinear BIP and ILP problems. In the future, they could potentially ​​integrate commercial solvers (e.g., Gurobi, SCIP) to enhance large-scale BIP optimization.

We thank the reviewers for their feedback. We believe we have addressed the reviewer’s main concerns about the novelty of this paper. We are happy to provide additional clarifications and engage further in the discussions if we have misunderstood any crucial points.

Many thanks, The Authors.

1. Gurobi & SCIP. Gurobi is designed to solve linear programming (LP) and quadratic programming (QP). While SCIP is outperformed by Gurobi in solving LP and QP problems, SCIP provides capabilities for handling general non-linear BIP problems.

2. DiffILO [1]. DiffILO is an unsupervised method with performance that can exceed Gurobi. Its methodology is the most similar to that of BIPNN. However, DiffILO employs bipartite graphs and GNNs to model constraints, whereas BIPNN utilizes HyperGNN to represent nonlinear BIPs. DiffILO is designed for linear BIPs, while BIPNN primarily addresses general nonlinear BIPs. Thus, our comparative analysis focuses on SCIP.

3. HypOp [2]. HypOp is an unsupervised methods. Compared with HypOp, ​​BIPNN first discovers the mapping correspondence between polynomials and hypergraphs structures​​. Compared to linear and quadratic problems, ​​the core challenge in solving nonlinear BIPs lies in exploiting GPU acceleration during training​​. BIPNN proposes a computational framework specifically for this purpose. ​​In contrast, HypOp utilizes distributed HyperGNN training​​, yet its hypergraph modeling solely targets constraints rather than objective functions, thus rendering HypOp ​​inapplicable to general BIP problems.

4. NeuralQP [3]. It is supervised and designed for QP problems. Supervised learning methods​​ require precomputing vast amounts of labels[1]. Obtaining labels for nonlinear BIPs is challenging, since ​​SCIP has higher computational overhead when solving nonlinear BIPs. Although NeuralQP demonstrates strong performance, it is specifically designed for QP problems. In contrast, BIPNN is designed for solving more complex nonlinear BIP problems, making it inherently difficult to match the performance of specialized QP solvers​​ such as NeuralQP.

​​5. MCPG [4] and VCA [5]. Reinforcement learning methods typically exhibit slow training convergence. MCPG [4] improves reinforcement learning algorithms and achieves strong performance on three problems: graph max-cut, MIMO, and MaxSAT. VCA also demonstrates its performance on TSP and graph max-cut problems. However, we observe that these studies exclusively evaluate on specific CO problems, making it difficult to assess whether their methods generalize to general BIPs.

For example, it seems that MCPG requires designing customized filters for specific problems, and we don't understand how to create filters for hypergraph max-cut or general BIP problems. BIPNN's novel GPU acceleration techniques; polynomial reformulation; and unconstrained optimization mechanisms may potentially enhance other methods.

We believe ​​BIPNN and DiffILO collectively address numerous limitations inherent in penalty-based deep learning methods​​ for solving nonlinear BIP and ILP problems. In the future, they could potentially ​​integrate commercial solvers (e.g., Gurobi, SCIP) to enhance large-scale BIP optimization.

summary.value: This paper introduces BIPNN, an unsupervised learning framework for solving nonlinear Binary Integer Programming (BIP) problems. Its core idea is to reformulate a complex, nonlinear, and constrained BIP into an unconstrained polynomial binary optimization (PUBO) problem via polynomial and penalty methods. This PUBO problem is then modeled as a hypergraph and solved end-to-end by a Hypergraph Neural Network (HyperGNN). To enhance scalability, the authors also design a GPU-accelerated training algorithm and an annealing strategy.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**

- The paper combines polynomial reformulation, hypergraph modeling, and unsupervised learning into a novel, end-to-end framework for the challenging class of nonlinear BIP problems.

- The proposed GPU-acceleration algorithm effectively addresses the computational bottleneck of large-scale PUBO loss functions, which is a key step toward practical application.

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper's claim that complex nonlinear terms can be used directly in the loss function is not well-explained and seems to conflict with the hypergraph modeling, which is based on polynomial interactions.

- The polynomial reformulation of functions like $\text{sin}(x_1+x_2)$ can introduce precision errors when variables are relaxed to the continuous space, a critical issue for problems with tight constraints that the paper fails to address.

- The paper does not adequately differentiate itself from recent and highly similar work using hypergraphs for optimization [1, 2], which weakens its originality claim.


- The evaluation omits comparisons with major commercial solvers (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX) and other specialized nonlinear solvers.

- Crucially, the paper lacks experiments on established public benchmarks for nonlinear optimization, such as QPLIB[3], which significantly undermines its performance claims.

- There is no discussion of the potential performance trade-offs of the chosen unsupervised approach versus supervised alternatives.

[1] Distributed constrained combinatorial optimization leveraging hypergraph neural networks.

[2] NeuralQP: A General Hypergraph-based Optimization Framework for Large-scale QCQPs.

[3] QPLIB: A library of quadratic programming instances.

- What is the impact of precision errors from the polynomial approximation during continuous relaxation, especially for problems with tight equality constraints?

- What are the key differences and advantages of BIPNN compared to recent, similar works like NeuralQP?

- Why was an unsupervised approach chosen? What is the expected performance trade-off compared to a supervised method?

summary.value: The authors propose a Hypergraph Neural Network (HyperNN) based solver for non-linear binary integer programming (BIP) problems. The proposed BIPNN approach reformulates BIP problems into unconstrained, differentiable and polynomial loss functions (PUBO formalism) that enable the training of a HyperGNN to solve these problems. This allows the method to be parallelizable on modern GPU hardware, making it significantly faster and more scalable than existing approaches. The authors provide clear explanations of how the BIP problems are reformulated into a unconstrained polynomial problem that can be used to train the HyperGNNs. An annealing strategy is used to ensure that the final solutions are binary. They show empirically that their method outperforms SOTA solvers on hypergraph max-cut problems and is comparable, sometimes outperforming) SOTA solvers on graph max-cut problems. They also show how the GPU parallelization enables their method to be significantly faster than SOTA solvers.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths
- The paper is generally very well written, most important concepts are clearly explained.
- The figures are well made and highly useful to clarify any concepts that might not be understood directly from the text itself.
- The proposed method is innovative.
- The empirical results properly showcase the benefits of the proposed methods.

### Weaknesses
While the paper is generally well written, some concepts could be better clarified:
- The precise "one-to-one" mapping between polynomial BIP objectives and hypergraph structures is mentioned multiple times throughout the text and in the abstract and while this mapping is somewhat intuitive from figure 1 it is not described precisely in the text. When the authors mention this in the abstract it gives the impression that there will be some mathematical results/ that shows the existence of this mapping. More details about this would be beneficial.
- A brief description of the inner workings of HyperGNNs would be useful to clarify these models for less familiar readers.
- While the training workflow is clear from the text and highly useful Fig 1, I feel like the paper would benefit from a brief intuitive explanation of how Eq. 4 works with the training.
- See the questions section for some others

questions.value:
### Questions
- The authors use the term "matrix" to refer to the PUBO matrix Q but this seems to be simply the vector of coefficients, naming it "matrix" introduces a bit of confusion so maybe "vector" would be a better term for clarity.
- How exactly does BIPNN generate a new hypergraph structure as opposed to the original hypergraph (Fig 3 & Sections 5 & 6)? This seems to be a central point in the experiments section but the phenomenon isn't clearly described. A brief discussion of how the generated hypergraph differs from the original one (perhaps with an example) would be beneficial.
- What exactly is the ratio of solutions? (Fig 4 & Section 6) Are the solutions here on the max-cut problem therefore the "solution" is the number of cuts and higher is better or is it the cost-function of the PUBO problem? This is unclear from the text.

summary.value:
This paper tries to solve a type of challenging optimization problem of nonlinear binary integer programming (BIP). This problem is fundamental in areas ranging from operations researches to chemical process control. It is hard problem due to its NP-completeness and the exploration of auxiliary variables in standard linearization schemes. 

By deriving a one-to-one mapping between polynomial BIP objectives and hyper graph structures, the authors propose a new method called BIPNN. It is an unsupervised hyper graph neural-network (HyperGNN) that can be used to tackle BIP. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness. 

The main contribution of this paper include
1) A systematic way to reformulate constrained, discrete, nonlinear IBs into unconstrained polynomial (PUBO) loss functions and encode nonlinearities (isn, log, etc.) via low-degree polynomials.
2) A continuous-annealing-enhanced training pipeline that performs gradient-based optimization end-to-end on the HyperGNN, avoiding costly branch-and-cut and auxiliary‐variable blowup. Also using GPU to speed up training. 
3) Good emperimental results on both synthetic hypergraphs (up to thousands of variables) and real-world graph/hypergraph max-cut benchmarks that BIPNN matches or outperforms other approaches in solution quality, while scaling well in time for fixed GPU resources .

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The main strengths include
1) Novel PUBO reformulation. The precise polynomial fitting of nonlinear terms for binary inputs enables an exact loss construction rather than heuristic linear relaxations .
2) End-to-End differentiable HyperGNN solver. Modeling multi-variable interactions as hyperedges and training HyperGNN directly on the PUBO loss bypasses expensive combinatorial search, achieving scalability and leveraging GPU parallelism.
3) Good empirical evaluation. Extensive benchmarks on both synthetic and real datasets, with comparisons against exact (SCIP) and heuristic (Tabu) solvers under a 1 hour limit, demonstrate BIPNN’s competitive performance, especially on larger instances.

The main weakness include 
1) Limited scalability of polynomial reformulation. The general transformation for multivariate nonlinearities causes exponential preprocessing in the number of variables per term, limiting applicability to only low-order interactions.
2) No clear reasons of HyperGNN architectural choices. While several HyperGNN variants are cited, the paper lacks ablation on how different architectures (HGNN+, HyperGCN, UniGCN) affect performance or how hyperparameters were selected. The author should provide hyperparameter guidelines. Provide systematic methods or default settings (and sensitivity analysis) for choose proper values of λ, μ, γ, etc. to aid reproducibility.
3) Weak Baselines. Comparison is confined to SCIP and Tabu, which are good open source code, but they are generally much worse than the MINLP solvers by Gurobi, FICO, etc. The baseline comparison should be strengthened by comparing with those solvers, so that the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach can be better justified.

questions.value:
On Page 1, "However, BIP is known to be NP-complete". This is not accurate. Assignment problems and shortest path are BIP, but has polynomial algorithm. This sentence can change to "However, BIP is generally known to be NP-complete"?

On page 5, Section 4.2, "where λ_k, μ_l are sufficiently large penalty coefficients".  What is the guidance on choosing the “sufficiently large” λ_k and μ_l to avoid infeasibility or poor convergence?

title.value: BIPNN: Learning to Solve Binary Integer Programming via Hypergraph Neural Networks

TLDR.value: This paper proposes a neural network-based binary integer programming solver.

abstract.value: Binary (0-1) integer programming (BIP) is pivotal in scientific domains requiring discrete decision-making. As the advance of AI computing, recent works explore neural network-based solver for integer linear programming (ILP) problems. Yet, they lack scalability for tackling nonlinear challenges. To handle nonlinearities, state-of-the-art Branch-and-Cut solvers employ linear relaxations, leading to exponential growth in auxiliary variables and severe computation limitations. To overcome these limitations, we propose BIPNN, an unsupervised learning framework to solve BIP problems via hypergraph neural networks (HyperGNN). Specifically, (i) BIPNN reformulates BIPs-constrained, discrete, and nonlinear (sin, log, exp) optimization problems-into unconstrained, differentiable, and polynomial loss functions. The reformulation stems from the observation of a precise one-to-one mapping between polynomial BIP objectives and hypergraph structures, enabling the unsupervised training of HyperGNN to optimize BIP problems in an end-to-end manner. On this basis, (ii) we propose a GPU-accelerated and continuous-annealing-enhanced training pipeline for BIPNN. The pipeline enables BIPNN to optimize large-scale nonlinear terms in BIPs fully in parallel via straightforward gradient descent, thus significantly reducing the training cost while ensuring the generation of discrete, high-quality solutions. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets highlight the superiority of our approach.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15)

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
